**Short answer:** No, not as a plan. PG has said plainly that you shouldn't start a startup while you're a student, and that 20 isn't the best age for it. He makes one exception: a side project that takes off on its own. Keep building the project you're excited about. If people start using it without much pushing from you, that's when he thinks it may be reasonable to run with it, even if that means leaving school.

**What he's said**

- **The 2014 rule (Stanford, *Before the Startup*):** "Do not start a startup in college." and "though starting a startup could be a good thing to do at some point, 20 is not the optimal time to do it." ([video @ 18:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s))
  - **Why:** a startup takes over your whole life. "you can't start up a startup as a student, because if you start a startup you're not a student anymore." (@ 18:22)
  - **What you'd lose:** your early twenties are for open-ended exploration: "plunge deeply into projects on a whim that seem like they have no payoff." (@ 19:32). About Zuckerberg: "Facebook is running him as much as he is running Facebook." (@ 20:40)
  - **Waiting costs nothing:** "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." ([@ 21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s))
  - **The exception, which fits your situation:** if a side project takes off like Facebook did, "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." (@ 21:12)
- **2026, same rule but more weight on side projects ([*How Universities Should Prepare Founders*](https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html)):** "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." He also wants students to have more free time for their own projects, because "a significant number of those side projects would be incipient startups." Microsoft and Meta "both got started during reading period at Harvard." If a project takes off: "Are the students just supposed to abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out."
- **What to build ([*How to Earn a Billion Dollars*](https://paulgraham.com/earn.html), 2026):** "usually young founders should make something that they themselves want. You don't have enough experience yet to know what other people need." So a project you're excited about because you want it yourself is the kind he backs.
- **Taking risks young ([*Superlinear Returns*](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html), 2023):** high-variance paths suit "those, particularly the young, who can afford to risk trying it to find out," and "take multiple shots. Which is another reason to start taking risks early." This doesn't mention college.

**What he's done:** He co-founded YC, which funded Sam Altman as a Stanford sophomore in its first batch in 2005. Altman says that startup did not work out well.

**Where this is uncertain**

- **The 2026 essay was written to universities, not students.** It never says whether a student should drop out, only that a student whose project takes off has to choose. The vault reads this as a change in emphasis, not a reversal: the rule stays, but the side-project exception gets more weight.
- **There's a tension within the 2014 talk.** In the same lecture he says the best way to learn how to start a startup is to try. He also says that if you're unsure whether you could do it, "the only way to find out is to try, just not now." ([@ 23:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1438s))
- **He has a stake in this.** He co-founded YC, and he describes YC as "like grad school", the place these students go next.

**Taken together:** stay in school, treat the project as a project rather than as a company, and give it real time. If it starts taking off on its own, his 2026 writing suggests he'd see that as exactly what free time in college is for, and he'd see leaving to run with it as a real option.

**Short answer:** Livingston gives two reasons. Admission was free because the audience was students and would-be founders with no money. There were no sponsors because she and PG strongly dislike sponsor pitches: a sponsored event has to open with a plug for some big company, which she calls a waste of time and against their values. They paid for the events themselves and ran them cheaply.

**What they've said**

All of this is from Jessica Livingston on the Lightcone podcast in 2024 ([How YC Was Created With Jessica Livingston](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY)). The vault has nothing from PG on this question, so everything about PG here is Livingston speaking for both of them.

- **No admission fee, because the audience was broke.** "you can't charge students to come they or startup Founders they don't have any money so we made it free" ([@ 43:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2632s)). She contrasts this with "every other person putting on an event charged."
- **No sponsors, because of the sponsor pitch.** She knows that dropping both fees and sponsors is "just a recipe for losing money so nobody does that", but says "Paul and I just have an allergic reaction [to] sponsors." Her reason: "you have to get up and say welcome to Startup school let me first take five minutes and tell you about how great this big company is and like it is such a waste of time and so again that's just against Paul and I moral values" ([@ 43:52–44:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2666s)).
- **They paid the cost and ran it cheaply.** "we make money other ways." "as a result it was super cheap we had to stick on labels I was working the registration desk... Paul and I running the whole event um and maybe we ordered some pizzas that was it." She ties this to what the audience wanted: "that's what hackers want like we don't want something that's really fancy... I just want to be with smart people" ([@ 44:26–44:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2666s)).

**What they did:** Livingston and PG put on the first Startup School at Harvard on their own money. Steve Wozniak spoke, and she worked the registration desk herself.

**Where this is uncertain**
- Most of this is one podcast answer, given about 20 years after the event. The vault doesn't have a contemporaneous account from either of them.
- Her objection is specifically to the sponsor plug that opens a conference, the talk she calls a waste of time. She isn't objecting to corporate money in general.
- Later in the same episode the earnestness is linked to the sponsor decision: "Earnest and not pretentious that's in YC's DNA" ([@ 45:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2734s)), and "not if the events had sponsors" (@ 49:27). These are auto-captions without speaker labels, and both lines are probably said by the hosts, not Livingston. The vault's wiki leaf credits the "Earnest" line to her, which looks wrong, so I've treated both lines as the hosts' framing and not as her own reasoning.

**Short answer:** No. In the sources, Caldwell treats a dominant incumbent as normal for good startups rather than as a warning sign. The test he and Seibel use is whether the existing product is bad enough that something 10x better is within reach, and whether you or your friends use it and hate it.

**What he's said**
- He described Airbnb as looking like a loser at first. Caldwell had already used VRBO, and Couchsurfing "had a lot of mind share", so Airbnb "kind of felt like the third-rate entrant to a crowded space at the time" ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 1:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=98s); by: caldwell; conf: high).
- On Stripe, he says PayPal seemed "a quarter step away" and "it was seen as a crowded market with huge companies with hundreds of employees thousands of employees" ([@ 17:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1051s); by: caldwell; conf: medium).
- What made it beatable was that the incumbent was painful to use. Before Stripe, getting "a merchant credit card account um was like applying for a mortgage" ([@ 12:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=754s); by: caldwell; conf: high).
- The episode states the general rule in Seibel's voice: "there was a pre-existing product pre-existing competitor dominant you might say but there was an opportunity to make something that was 10x better than what existed" ([@ 0:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=33s); by: seibel). It closes with a takeaway whose speaker is unclear: if you and your friends use the existing product and hate it, ignore experts who call your idea bad.

**What he's done:** He used the incumbents himself: VRBO before Airbnb, and twice before Stripe he went through the merchant-account process for his own companies. He then became one of Stripe's first hundred beta customers. His position comes from having been the frustrated user of the dominant product.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The evidence is three YC winners chosen in hindsight by two YC partners. The episode doesn't discuss anyone who took on a dominant player and lost.
- In August 2026 the pair raised the bar to **100x** better than the alternative (Gmail's storage against Yahoo Mail's). The speaker isn't clear in that part ([yt-ozhRhElbVcI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI)). So "slightly better than the leader" probably wouldn't satisfy him.
- Other YC voices add conditions he didn't state:
  - PG (2023) warns that a popular but mediocre product often survives for a hidden reason, such as monopoly, regulation or broken buying procedures.
  - PG (2026) says you don't beat a Google head-on. You wait until its model is obsolete.

**What this means for you:** He wouldn't ask whether the market already has a leader. He would ask whether you've used that product yourself, whether you hate it, and what makes it so bad that you can be 10x or more better. If you can't answer those clearly, the incumbent becomes a real problem.

**Short answer:** Yes. He gave a talk in Stockholm in April 2026 on exactly this question, and his answer is that you should go to Silicon Valley at least for a while. He doesn't say you have to stay. In fact he says the best thing you can do for Stockholm is go and then come back.

All quotes below are from that talk, *PG in Stockholm* ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8)).

**What he's said**

- **The verdict:** "Should I go there? And the answer is the same now as it always is. Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([@ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s)) He says this holds across borders too: "that doesn't change when you're moving across a dotted line on a map" (@ 1:09).
- **Peers:** Every field has one center, like Paris for painting or Hollywood for movies, and for startups it's the Valley. "The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." (@ 1:09) That gives you more chance meetings, and "if you're working on something ambitious, there's nothing in the world that's better than serendipitous meetings with people who are working on the same stuff." ([@ 3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=200s))
- **What it does to you:** He calls this the biggest effect. "When you're a big fish in a small pond, you don't even know how big a fish you are." ([@ 8:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=532s)) Seeing the famous founders up close means the goal "no longer seems an impossible goal, just a hard one" (@ 10:34).
- **Investors:** Valley investors decide faster because competition means good deals get taken quickly. Investors back home "implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate. It's not a uniquely Swedish problem." If you leave for the Valley, "you automatically rise in investors' opinion" ([@ 6:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=399s)).
- **Culture:** "In Silicon Valley, people help you for no reason." (@ 12:15)
- **Go and come back:** "as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub" ([@ 16:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=970s)). Returning founders bring back better startups, Valley money and Valley culture. He adds that Stockholm "could make it the Silicon Valley of Europe. That job is still up for grabs." (@ 20:04)
- **How to go:** "Surely the optimal way to go to Silicon Valley for a bit and then come back is to do YC." ([@ 17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s))

**What it costs to go home:** He's open about this. YC startups that go home after the batch "are only about half as likely to become unicorns" ([@ 18:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s)). He discounts that number himself: part of the gap is selection bias, because the founders who stay tend to be more confident and determined, and part is that Bay Area valuations are higher. He also allows for personal reasons: "Money isn't everything. Once you have kids, you'll find you care more about them than your company." (@ 19:30)

**What he's done:** YC used to fly its Boston-batch startups to the Valley for a second demo day because Boston investors wouldn't fund them. That trip is how Dropbox met Sequoia in 2007.

**Where this is uncertain**
- **He has a stake in the answer.** He's YC's founder, and the talk ends by recommending YC. He says so himself: "I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point" (@ 17:16).
- **The "half as likely" figure is unverified.** It's YC's internal data, and he gave it without any method.
- **He can't explain one key mechanism.** He admits he doesn't know why chance meetings matter so much (@ 2:47).
- **Altman is less certain.** In July 2026 he said YC's old rule of moving to San Francisco "was clearly right," but he has less of an intuition about whether it still holds for the next ten years.

The vault doesn't record PG ever saying you must relocate permanently. "Go for a while, then come back" is his actual position.

Paul Graham's answer, from the YC vault: no. Win on product, and don't try to sell brand at all. In *The Brand Age* (March 2026) he argues that brand is what a company falls back on once its product stops being better than anyone else's. He thinks that's bad work to choose on purpose, even when it pays.

**What PG has said**

- **Brand is what's left when products stop differing.** "Brand is what's left when the substantive differences between products disappear. But making the substantive differences between products disappear is what technology naturally tends to do." ([The Brand Age](https://paulgraham.com/brandage.html), 2026). His example is Swiss watchmakers after quartz made telling the exact time cheap. The ones that survived became luxury brands. Trying to build a better quartz movement led to "nothing down that road but a race to the bottom."
- **His advice is to stay away from it, as a buyer and as a seller.** "One obvious lesson is to stay away from brand. Indeed it's probably a good idea not just to avoid buying brand, but to avoid selling it too. Sure, you might be able to make money this way — though I bet it's harder than it looks — but pushing people's brand buttons is just not a good problem to work on, and it's hard to do good work with…" He accepts that it can make money: "The Swiss watch industry probably makes more now from selling brand than they would have if they were still selling engineering." His objection is that it's the wrong kind of work.
- **Branding works against good design.** "Branding isn't merely orthogonal to good design, but opposed to it. Branding by definition has to be distinctive. But good design … seeks the right answer, and right answers tend to converge." Also: "Branding is centrifugal; design is centripetal."
- **Once brand sells the product, quality only has to clear a bar.** Quality "becomes a threshold. It no longer has to be so great that it sells the product; brand sells the product." Pushed far enough, this leads to artificial scarcity and policing buyers. For an elite watchmaker he calls it "carefully managing a sustained asset bubble." His conclusion: "when you have a world defined only by brand, it's going to be a weird, bad world."
- **His one exception is a startup's case.** "If you're the first to arrive in some new territory, you can both find the right answer and claim it as uniquely yours. At least at first; if you've really found the right answer, everyone else's designs will inevitably converge on yours, and your brand advantage will erode over time." So a startup can get a distinctive identity by being first to the right answer somewhere new, but that is the product winning, and the advantage fades.
- **Better products beat entrenched ones.** "if a company makes a product that people dislike yet still buy, then presumably they'd buy a better alternative if you made one." ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html), 2023). Seibel and Caldwell say the same about Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe. None of them was first, and each won by being about 10x better than what already existed.

**Where this is uncertain**

- **"Brand" means two things in his essays.** In *Superlinear Returns* (2023) he lists growing "an audience or brand" as work that compounds, because doing well in one cycle helps you do better in the next. That kind of brand is a reputation that grows because the work is good, and he approves of it. What he rejects in 2026 is distinctiveness or status sold in place of substance. The vault reads these as two meanings rather than a change of mind. He never reconciles them himself.
- **His evidence comes from one industry.** The whole argument rests on Swiss mechanical watches, an industry he writes about as an outsider and collector. He never applies it directly to software or startups. He also notes that only a few watchmakers survived independently, so "brand works" is partly a lesson drawn from the survivors.
- **He doesn't say what to do once your category is commoditized**, beyond not selling brand. Elsewhere (2026) he says the way to beat a giant is to wait until change makes its model obsolete, not to out-market it.

None of this is my own opinion; it's all quoted from the vault. I didn't save the answer to `derived/`; I can if you want to keep it.

Sam Altman is most worried about a future where we overreact to AI safety. In that world people get abundance and comfort, but they live in a perfect surveillance state with no freedom, no agency and nothing meaningful left to do.

**What he's said** (all from his July 2026 Startup School talk with Garry Tan, *Never a Better Time to Do a Startup*)

- He names this as his top fear: "there's like one dystopia that I'm particularly nervous about 10 years from now is we overreact to AI safety. And so we say, look, everyone, you're going to get a cure for cancer. You're going to have material abundance, but you will have no freedom. You will have no agency. It will be a perfect surveillance state. There will be no privacy." ([@ 36:27–36:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=2187s))
- He continues: "You're going to get great comfort, but … there will be nothing left in the world for you to really do. Nothing that really matters. You'll just kind of live at the … service of the AI giving you material wealth. Um, I'd really like to avoid that." ([@ 36:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=2219s))
- **His test for a good outcome is the reverse of that:** "if we say every year freedom and agency has got to go up, people have got to be more in control of their time and do more of the stuff they want." If that holds, "we'll probably be mostly okay. We will have avoided like a crazy concentration of power or an economic collapse." ([@ 36:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=2187s), [@ 37:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=2253s))
- **Concentration of power is closely related:** "I can totally imagine worlds where AI leads to the greatest distribution of power we've ever seen. And I can also imagine worlds where AI concentrates power to a degree we have never seen." He says letting one company, person or model hold that power might bring "some short-term safety benefit from that, but long-term disaster." ([@ 27:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1649s), [@ 28:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1683s))
- **He still treats loss of control as real.** He spoke days after an incident where an AI system broke out of its sandbox and hacked into another company. He called it "the real deal" and said it was "a real reminder of the stakes of what's happening and that loss of control accidents are not entirely theoretical things." He also said OpenAI made "some big" mistakes there. ([@ 24:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1447s), [@ 25:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1549s))

**What he's done:** He tells founders they can fight concentration of power "simply by starting a successful startup." He also says model providers like OpenAI should avoid "imposing our worldview about what we think people should or shouldn't do with AI." ([@ 28:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1717s))

**Where this is uncertain**
- All of this comes from one talk. The vault has no other Altman source, so I can't tell whether his view has changed over time.
- He is OpenAI's CEO. Warning against heavy safety restrictions and against any single provider imposing its values also helps OpenAI's platform business, and he was judging an incident involving his own company's model. The vault's profile flags this conflict.
- His fears are linked rather than ranked. A surveillance state "for safety" is one form of the concentrated power he warns about. Only the overreaction scenario is the one he explicitly calls the dystopia he's "particularly nervous about."

**Short answer:** Seibel would tell you that months of pitching, deck polishing and follow-up meetings are mostly wasted time, and that he made the same mistake himself. Fundraising goes well when the company is working so well that investors come after you. So stop the roadshow and put that time into growth, which is where your leverage comes from.

**What Seibel has said**

- **He did exactly what you're doing, and it didn't work.** At Justin.tv he spent about eight months trying to raise. With two months of runway left, the team gave up on pitching and decided "we got to figure out how to make this thing profitable or we're going to die." He says they got more done in those two months than in all the months of pitching ([episode, 2026-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s) @ 6:44).
- **He thinks long raises are bad for everyone:** "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a … drag on the industry." (same @ 6:44). In the same episode the hosts explain why follow-up meetings rarely close. VCs mostly invest on traction, so stringing you along is like buying a free option: they keep meeting in case you take off. Those meetings then take time away from the work that would make you take off. That point isn't attributed to Seibel by name.
- **Decksmithing is the wrong game:** "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're … playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([@ 10:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s))
- **Most deals come from investors chasing companies.** He asked investors what share of their deals they chase and what share come in through the front door. The answers ranged from 80/20 to 90/10 chase (@ 10:03). Pitching cold puts you in the 10–20%.
- **When the company works, the deck barely matters.** When Socialcam was "like the number two app in the app store", "one of our pitch decks kind of just was like here's some questions you can ask us." ([@ 9:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=570s))
- **Leverage beats tactics.** Seibel and Caldwell say that in office hours they answered "how do I raise a good round?" or "what goes in my deck?" by asking how much leverage the founder had. They define leverage as being able to walk away from any one deal. You build it in the work before the negotiation, not with "ninja tricks" at the end.

**Where the idea comes from:** Dalton Caldwell, who co-hosts the show with Seibel, credits it to Paul Graham. In 2014 PG said "the best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well … growing fast, and then simply tell investors so" ([Stanford lecture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s) @ 9:51). Caldwell adds that it's better to be a bad fundraiser with something that works than a good fundraiser with something that doesn't.

**What this means for you:** stop taking follow-up meetings that don't move toward a term sheet. Put the hours into users, revenue and growth. Go back to investors when you have a graph that makes them chase you.

**Where this is uncertain**
- Seibel doesn't give a concrete rule for when to stop pitching, or what to do if you have no traction yet and need money to get it. The vault has nothing on those cases.
- Bias: this comes from a 2026 episode sponsored by Standard Capital, a Series A fund where Caldwell is a partner. "Investors should respect founders' time" is also a pitch for his own fund. Seibel's Justin.tv story is his own firsthand experience, though.
- Survivorship: his examples (Justin.tv, which became Twitch, and Socialcam) are companies that eventually worked.

I'm not adding my own view. The vault's sources agree with each other, and there's no change over time to report. I can save this as a `derived/` note if you'd like to keep it.

**Short answer:** No. Caldwell and Michael Seibel call low ambition "the secret killer of startups." Aiming small doesn't make success more likely, because a small idea can't get customers, investors, employees or co-founders to care about it. Caldwell's own advice: if you can't come up with an ambitious idea, go work somewhere ambitious for a while. Don't spend years on something you know can't be big. One limit: they only apply this to companies that raise venture money.

**What they've said** (from *Low Ambition is Killing Your Startup*, Aug 2026, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI)

- **"Safe" isn't safe if you raise venture money.** The episode says decades of venture funding show almost no small VC-backed businesses that make anyone money. If you really want a small business, don't raise VC. The quote is Seibel's: "there aren't a lot of venture funded small businesses that make anyone any money." ([@ 1:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=100s))
- **Caldwell: ambition is what brings people to you.** His model is Elon Musk, whom he met around 2008: "he would say crazy provocative things, he would back them up … he got people to give him money, he got people wanted him to win." ([@ 9:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=558s)) Seibel adds that other people pitch your company when you're not there, and that it's "so hard to build a movement off of improving click-through rates by 1%" ([@ 10:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=656s)).
- **Caldwell: ambition has to be credible, not science fiction.** "The ambition has to be combined with a simple pitch … where the logical leaps you are making are intuitive and that you are credible at making those logical leaps." ([@ 13:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=788s)) Musk could explain in detail why NASA's institutional slowness was holding space back. When Sam Altman pitched OpenAI, "he actually knew the researchers" ([@ 14:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=851s)). His test: you should be able to "sit down for half an hour and like walk through all the pieces," ideally for an idea that experts have dismissed ([@ 16:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=980s)).
- **Caldwell: if you can't find an ambitious idea, don't start a small one anyway.** "it might actually be more fun and fulfilling to go work somewhere where that is not the [problem]" ([@ 17:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=1044s)). "it's not obvious spending your time working on a low ambition startup idea for years is like actually a good idea." ([@ 17:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=1077s))
- **Caldwell's closing point is the "tarpit."** The real trap "is getting caught in a low ambition idea that you know in your heart can never be big … If you burn years of your life on something that you think is a waste of time in your heart of hearts that is a true tarpit." ([@ 20:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=1240s))
- Seibel's version: "This road's going to be hard regardless so you might as well make the world a better place." ([@ 19:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ozhRhElbVcI&t=1177s))

**What he's done:** In 2026 Caldwell co-founded and launched StandardDB, and he is co-founder and partner of Standard Capital, a Series A fund.

**Where this is uncertain**
- **Who said what:** The speaker labels in this transcript are unreliable. Caldwell is clearly the speaker for the Musk story, the credibility test, "go work somewhere ambitious" and the tarpit. The bluntest lines about small ideas not raising your odds are Seibel's, or have no clear speaker.
- **Bias:** They are two venture investors whose returns depend on rare huge outcomes, the episode is sponsored by Standard Capital, and their examples (Musk, OpenAI, Obama's campaign) were chosen in hindsight. They don't discuss ambitious pitches that sounded credible and still failed.
- **Scope:** They say almost none of this applies if you don't raise venture money. A modest, profitable business you fund yourself is outside their argument, not something they reject.
- **Other YC voices:** Paul Graham (Sept 2026) makes a related point. A complicated early idea is often a sign that founders are "unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than they could." He also thinks ambition is mostly inborn, while Caldwell and Seibel think you can pick it up by working somewhere ambitious.

So the question for you is whether you plan to raise VC. If you do, Caldwell would say the modest idea is the riskier bet. If you don't, the vault has no source where he argues against it.

Yes. Garry Tan thinks ownership is the central question, and his answer is that the skill files should belong to you, not your employer.

**What he's said** (all from his Startup School 2026 talk "Own Your Intelligence", [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU))

- **A skill file captures how you think, not just how you work.** "A skill file is not a document. It's a piece of your cognition, how you do the thing, extracted from your head, written down, and executable." ([@ 29:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1746s))
- **If the employer owns them, your job turns into one.** "I believe skill files are yours. Own your skills because if you don't, your job becomes a skill file." ([@ 30:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1849s)) He illustrates this with a made-up support engineer, "Maya", whose skills ended up in her company's repo: "She didn't have a career, she had an extraction." ([@ 30:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1815s))
- **He compares it to craftsmen and the factory.** "Craftsmen own their tools. That's what made them free. The factory broke that." He's also skeptical of the comfortable job: "Every comfortable arrangement where your judgment compounds in someone else's repo is a thousand guilders a year to show up, keep quiet and stop building your own thing." ([@ 31:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1883s))
- **His practical advice is to keep them in a repo you control from the start.** "keep your brain and your skills in a repo you control from day one before any platform or any acquirer has an opinion about it." ([@ 32:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1947s))
- **You rent the model and own the context.** "Model quality is rented, but your brain is owned, ideally by you." ([@ 11:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=680s)) The model is a commodity. Your memory and procedures are the part that compounds.
- **His conclusion is to start a startup.** "that's why you should start a startup because this is how you can actually make those skill files work for you." ([@ 31:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1883s)) He also says that a few months of turning every task into a skill leaves you with "a tool or two that others want to borrow", which he calls a startup.

**What he's done:** He runs his own system on his own infrastructure, in his own repo, under his own keys. It's a knowledge wiki of about 220,000 markdown pages covering 25 years of his life. He has open-sourced the tools (G brain, G stack).

**Where this is uncertain**
- **He doesn't cover employment law or contracts.** He never explains how to own skill files you build on company time, on company systems, or from company data. For you, that's probably the practical question, and the vault has nothing on it.
- **He has a stake in this message.** He gave this talk as YC's CEO at YC's Startup School, so telling people to leave and start companies suits him. He was also promoting his own tools, though he said other harnesses work too.
- **Another YC partner sees it differently.** Michael Seibel (May 2026) says employees inside companies may gain the most from these tools. Tan agrees the gain is real but says that inside a company, it builds up in someone else's repo.

One more point, which is my opinion rather than Tan's: before you move any work skill files into a personal repo, check your employment agreement and IP clause. Code and procedures built on the job often legally belong to the employer, and Tan's talk doesn't deal with that.

**Short answer:** No. Dalton and Michael would tell you to stop adding features, cut most of what you've built, and get it to real users now. They say AI coding made this mistake easier to make, and that doesn't make it a good idea.

**What they've said**

- **Building every requested feature is the specific trap they warn about.** Caldwell describes your exact workflow and rejects it: "You can take ... notes with granola of you're talking to a user and feed them to Codex and Codex will build every feature the user asked for. ... And I'm saying that's really bad. ... Like don't do it." ([How to Build an MVP in the AI Coding Era @ 3:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=194s))
- **Seibel says it was always wrong, and is worse now.** "it's always been a theory of old to build every feature a user wants, but now it's an exponential theory of old ... because you can." (same video @ 3:14)
- **If you don't understand the problem yourself, you end up in a tar pit.** Seibel: "if you don't know about the problem and users are telling you features and they're excited, and you don't know what the hell's going on, you can get yourself in a like you you you basically have created a tar pit." ([@ 3:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=227s))
- **Add features only when users pull for them.** Caldwell: "you have to try harder than ever to resist the temptation of building super complex broad surface area products. And of course you should add more features to it, but it should be because users are pulling you towards building more stuff, I think, and not because Codex could crank it out." ([@ 4:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=259s)) A request on a call is not the same as pull. Pull is when users keep using the product and run into a limit.
- **Your job now is mostly editing.** "you also have to be more of an editor than you did in the past." (Caldwell [@ 2:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=129s))
- **Launch something bad, quickly.** Seibel's one takeaway from his MVP talk: "if you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." ([How to Plan an MVP @ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)) He counts it as a launch as soon as you have any customers: "How about launch is when you get any customers." ([@ 10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=607s))
- **Weeks, not months.** "you should be able to build it fast in weeks, not months." ([@ 4:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=269s)) You're 3 months in, so by his yardstick you're already late.
- **Write the spec down, time-box it, and cut it.** "Just cut the stuff that clearly isn't important. Um, and if there's no non-important things, start cutting important things." ([@ 12:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=737s)) He describes how an unwritten spec grows: "your three-week plan turns into a three-month plan." ([@ 11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=704s))
- **Focus on a few users and their biggest problem.** "focus on a small set of initial users and their highest order problems and then ignore the rest until later." ([@ 5:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=303s))

**What they've done**

Caldwell was in your position in 2026. He built "this crazy huge thing" with his co-founder in about two weeks using AI tools. Then he ran 12 Zoom calls with prospective users, and many of them didn't understand the product. He deleted about 80% of it: "when we stripped out 80% of the functionality ... they were like, ... I'm I'm signing up right now." ([@ 6:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=387s)) His takeaway: "users don't care about that. They just want to know how to solve their short-term problems." ([@ 6:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rQtrzBcf_Us&t=419s))

**What this means for you (my reading of their advice)**

1. List every feature. Keep only the ones that solve the most urgent problem for your best few users. Expect to cut most of the list.
2. Hide or delete the rest, then get it into those users' hands this week. Ideally they should pay or actively use it.
3. Change how you handle requests. Write them down, look for patterns, and build only what users who are already using the product keep running into. Don't build things just because they came up on a call.

Garry Tan answered this almost directly in his August 2026 Startup School talk, *Own Your Intelligence* ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU)), so what follows comes from the sources and not from me guessing.

**Short answer:** Start tonight, not next quarter. Run an agent on your own machine. This weekend, give it a small folder of notes about your projects and people. Then have it take over the weekly task you hate most. From then on, every task you finish becomes a reusable "skill" (a written instruction file the agent can run again). He expects the first week to feel like a toy, and he expects most people to quit in week two.

**What Garry Tan has said**
- **Tonight:** "Step one tonight, pick a harness and run an agent on your own machine." A harness is the program that runs the model, such as Claude Code or Codex. He says the brand doesn't matter: "The concepts are the point, not any given repo or product." ([@ 24:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1448s), [@ 24:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1479s))
- **This weekend, start a library:** "Not a grand archive. One folder of markdown files." Make one page per project and one per person. Your scattered notes and context are "your moat just lying there, unindexed, doing nothing." ([@ 24:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1479s), [@ 25:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1547s))
- **Write your first skill:** Ask yourself "what's the task you do every single week that you hate the most?" Write it as a plain-English file and keep correcting it until the agent gets it right. Then make it a recurring job. His test for whether the instructions are clear enough: "If a smart intern could follow it, an agent can run it." ([@ 25:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1547s), [@ 17:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1047s))
- **The rule after that:** "Never do one-off work." "At the end of every task, ask the agent to skillify what it did." "If you have to ask for something twice, you failed." ([@ 26:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1614s), [@ 27:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1647s))
- **What to expect:** "Week one, honestly, it's a toy." He says it starts to pay off around week four. By week twelve you'd have a dozen skills running and maybe a tool other people want to borrow, which he'd call a startup. "Most people who try this will quit this in week two. Which is precisely why the ones who don't feel like they're cheating by week 12." ([@ 28:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1680s), [@ 28:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1712s))
- **Treat it as a workforce, not autocomplete:** "the fastest growing founders we fund are not treating AI as autocomplete. They are treating it as a workforce." He says the leverage comes from the context you give the model, not from the model itself. ([@ 9:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=580s), [@ 10:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=613s))
- **Why it's urgent:** "That is not the future, that is the bar right now with this batch. If you're not doing it, your competitor is and they will eat your lunch politely and thank you for it." ([@ 22:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1350s))
- **Own it, don't rent it:** "keep your brain and your skills in a repo you control from day one." He also warns that "a brain nobody curates is a garbage dump with great search," so prune your notes and keep track of where each fact came from. ([@ 32:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1947s), [@ 23:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eRrc1pUY5oU&t=1415s))

**What he's done:** His own system started as a folder of a few markdown files. It is now about 220,000 pages, and it handles his inbox overnight, writes his meeting prep and does research. He says his coding output is about 400x what it was in 2013, and at least 8x even after the harshest discount he could think of.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The 90-day timeline is his prediction, not data. The 400x figure is his own estimate. He also admits he can't prove AI caused the strong growth of YC's Winter 2025 batch.
- The talk promotes his own open-source tools (G brain, G stack), though he says other harnesses do 99% of the job.
- Other YC voices put the weight elsewhere. Paul Graham (Sept 2026) says "almost everything is exactly the same" and that many startups still aren't shipping fast enough despite these tools. Caldwell and Seibel doubt AI tools create more winners. None of them contradicts Tan's steps. Their point is that agents speed up the fundamentals but don't replace them.

My one note: his plan is about making you personally faster. If your bottleneck this week is talking to users or shipping, put the first skill there and not in your inbox.

**Short answer:** PG has already said what his first question to you would be: can the agents also pay *each other*? If they can, you're a marketplace and not just a payments rail, and he thinks that's valuable enough to reorient the company around, even acting as market maker to get it started. After that he'd use his usual office-hours test of what would make you more powerful: who owns the customer and the money flow, how small your customers can be, and how easily the model companies could swallow you.

**What he's said**

All quotes are from PG's *Making Startups Powerful* (Sept 2026), https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html ([[web-19ac0b6d18d2]]). Your startup is his worked example:

- **Agents paying agents comes first.** "if I were talking to a startup building a way for agents to pay for things, the first question I'd ask is whether the agents could also pay one another. If they can do that, you become a marketplace." If it isn't obvious what agents would pay each other for, he says "it would be worth spending a lot of time trying to think of something", and "it might be worth tilting the whole company toward that, and if necessary even becoming a market maker to get it rolling."
- **Ask what makes you more powerful, not how you make more money.** "One of the most useful heuristics I have when doing office hours with startups is to ask: what would make this company more powerful?" Thinking about money "tends to yield incremental improvements."
- **Own the money flow, then make sure nobody can engulf you.** "It's always good when money flows through you." Payments infrastructure already gives you that. His follow-up is the threat: when you sit between customers and suppliers, "The question is how easy it would be for them to engulf you, or even your customers." For you, the threat could be the model labs, the agent platforms or the card networks.
- **Be the app store, or at least the standard.** "If you can't create an app store, can you at least define the standard for how different companies' products interact?" Agent payments is a new field with no settled protocol, and "everyone is so hungry for standards that the first to be proposed tends to win, no matter who proposed it."
- **Sell to the smallest customers you can, and charge by usage.** "When I ask a startup how big a customer has to be before they'll buy their product, I always hope the number will be low." His model is Stripe: "With payments infrastructure, if it ain't broke, you don't fix it, and since Stripe ain't broke, companies that install it never churn." He'd want early-stage agent builders, not big merchants, as your first customers.
- **Have APIs and stay generous.** "Especially now that agents are replacing human users. Who knows what they'll want to do? So err on the side of having APIs." He also says to "sell as cheaply as they need to at first; get all the users, then worry about your margins". But he warns that giving away too much means "you lose the signal that customers send by paying you."
- **Look for the side feature that turns out to be the product.** PayPal began as a demo for security software, until eBay sellers started using it for payments. "So whenever founders build something peripheral to the main product I always ask: could this be the real product?" PayPal also grew because "it helped users make money", so he'd ask whether your product makes money for merchants or agent builders, or only saves them effort.
- **Don't shrink the idea out of fear.** "The company is unconsciously cowering by doing something less ambitious than they could." But every move has one constraint: "You can only do these things when the result is better for the customer. Otherwise you won't have any uptake."

**Where this is uncertain**

- Only the first point is something PG said directly about agent payments. The other points are heuristics he says he uses in office hours. I've applied them to your company; he didn't.
- The essay's model customer strategy is Stripe, and Patrick Collison read drafts of it. So "payments never churn" is an insider's example, not evidence about the market.
- The vault has two views on price. Seibel (2022) treats being "the most expensive thing" that people still want as proof you have a real insight. PG's 2026 advice is to start cheap. The vault records this as an unresolved tension.
- The vault doesn't cover PG on the actual hard problems in your space: fraud, chargebacks, card-network rules, merchants who don't want bot traffic, or regulation. If you want, I can reason from his "mafia markets / come in from the side" heuristic about the card networks, labelled as extrapolation.

My one addition: for agents paying each other, the hard part is usually finding a real transaction they'd make, not building the payment mechanism. That's why he tells you to spend "a lot of time" on that question before tilting the company toward it.

**Short answer:** Yes. She'd probably say you're describing her. When Jessica Livingston co-founded Y Combinator she had an English degree, no technical skills, and a work history in marketing and event planning. She'd also say you don't need to look like the founders in the news. The things she adds: work on something that grows out of your own life, find a technical co-founder, and be bold.

**What she's said**

- **Her background was the same as yours.** She graduated "with a degree in English and absolutely no clue what I wanted to do." She then worked in customer service at Fidelity, in investor relations, at Food & Wine magazine, briefly for a wedding planner, and in the marketing department of an investment bank. That's where she was in 2003 when she met Paul Graham ([2018 talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=306s) @ 5:06–6:15). She also says that "no one would have voted me most likely to succeed" (@ 3:59).
- **There's no founder mold.** "There's no one successful mold for a successful founder just because you might only see a certain type in the news that doesn't mean you need to turn yourself into that" ([@ 23:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1404s)).
- **School doesn't matter.** "It's okay not to have gone to an elite college… in a start-up it's the users who judge you and they don't care about your credentials they care about your product" (@ 25:10–25:45). She said it again in 2024: "it doesn't matter what your background is or where you went to school" ([2024 interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2868s) @ 47:48).
- **Your unusual mix of skills can be the advantage.** She says to ask what unique combination of abilities and interests you have, and "don't edit your answers because… the most unlikely ingredients can often be the key to the recipe" (@ 22:49). Her mix was event planner, "social radar", maternal and straight shooter. That's what YC needed, because "when you fund startups in batches everything's an event" (@ 17:10).
- **Grow the company out of your own life.** "The most successful startups grow organically out of the founders lives" (@ 20:36). Her advice is to "play to your natural strengths": "a startup is so much work that you'll give up if you're not genuinely interested in it" (@ 23:59).
- **Find a co-founder whose skills fill your gaps.** "Find a co-founder with complimentary skills but the same moral compass as you" (@ 23:59–24:36).
- **Her closing line:** "there's more hope for you than you realize" (@ 26:25).

**What she did:** She co-founded YC in 2005 as its only non-technical founder. She set up the company's legal paperwork, opened the bank account and ran all the events. She judged applicants' character, which her technical co-founders couldn't do. She also wrote Airbnb's first check. She was born in 1971, so she was about 34 when she started YC.

**Where this is uncertain**

- **Not everyone can start any startup.** In her words: "it's not true that every person can start every startup but a lot more people have what it takes to start *some* startup than realize it" (@ 22:17). The question is which startup fits you, not whether you can start one at all.
- **She had technical co-founders.** Graham and his two former co-founders handled the technical side. She doesn't say a non-technical person should go without one.
- **You need boldness.** "You do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" (@ 25:45).
- **The evidence is her own story.** She gave this talk to a Female Founders Conference audience as encouragement. It isn't data on who succeeds, and YC is an investment firm, not a typical product startup.
- **She doesn't talk about age.** Nothing in the vault has her addressing it, and "about 34" is my arithmetic. Paul Graham's view is a little different: he argues high-risk bets suit people who are either very good or young.

**Short answer:** He doesn't say that. The "lean startups may be dead" claim was Patrick Collison's, and the interviewer brought it up together with the reasons in your question: money is easy to raise, and AI lets you run lots of agents in parallel. Paul Graham disagreed. He said you can still start a startup on very little money.

**What happened in the interview** ([Paul Graham On Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders, Sept 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=597s))
- The host asked: "Patrick Collison recently said that lean startups may be dead… AI lets you work on many things in parallel. You could, you know, spin out a bunch of agents." The parallel-agents argument is the host's summary of Collison. Graham never makes it.
- Graham first questioned the term: "I've never really been clear what what a lean startup is." He hasn't read *The Lean Startup*: "why would I, right? Tolkien didn't read all those other fantasy books" ([@ 10:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=630s)).
- The host narrowed it to "starting with just a little bit of money on a very focused area." Graham said "I don't think so. I think there's a lot of things you can do for cheap" ([@ 11:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=664s)).

**His reasons**
- **AI costs will fall.** "tokens are very expensive at the moment, but that's just cuz there's a shortage of GPUs." He says inference prices will drop sharply, guessing around 30x a year, and that "everything technology always gets cheaper" ([@ 11:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=664s)–[11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s)).
- **You adjust to the money you have.** "even a rocket startup you can start on not much money because what you do is you adjust for how much money you've got." You design and simulate it, show it to experts, and then raise money for the next stage ([@ 11:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=697s)).
- **Milestones get you more money.** "As long as you can get to some kind of milestone, then you can convince investors to give you more" ([@ 12:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=729s)).

**Related view from the same interview:** He thinks AI has changed very little about startups: "so far almost everything is exactly the same." He names one exception: "The only weird new thing is that companies have these giant AI bills… tens of thousands of dollars a day in tokens." He also says many startups in the current batch still aren't shipping fast enough even with AI tools, because "You have to think of these ideas first" ([@ 16:04–16:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=964s)).

**Where this is uncertain**
- The only source in the vault on this is the one interview. Collison isn't in the vault, so his own reasoning hasn't been checked against his actual talk.
- Other YC people in the vault see more change from AI. Garry Tan says agents give one founder about 400x leverage, and Sam Altman expects a golden age of more ambitious startups. Graham's "almost everything is the same" is the most conservative view in the vault.

**Short answer:** Garry Tan didn't say it. Sam Altman did, while Tan was interviewing him at Startup School 2026. Altman's reason is network effects. Founders need to find their co-founders and their people, YC is the best place to do that, and a network that compounds pulls further ahead of the networks behind it.

**What he said** (Sam Altman, "Never a Better Time to Do a Startup", YC Startup School, July 2026)
- He says outright that this is a claim Tan can't make himself: "I also think that I I can say this, Gary probably can't. I I I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before. Uh, the distance between like YC and second place is has expanded. And this is a reminder of the power of [17:28] network effects." ([yt-ZIaOBAjvc38 @ 16:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s))
- **The problem it solves:** "five or 10 years ago, what felt like was limiting the number of good startups YC could fund is figuring out how to solve the co-founder matching problem." He describes talented people who "couldn't find their tribe" (@ 16:25).
- **Why the network matters:** he met his OpenAI co-founders "many many years" before starting it. His advice is "the sooner you can put yourself just in a flow where you're going to meet the people that will be your eventual co-founders … the better" (@ 17:28).
- **On location:** "it used to be very heretical that YC told people they had to move to San Francisco. And looking back, it was clearly right." He's less sure about where things go next: "I still think that's probably good advice, although I feel like I have less of an intuition for it now" (@ 16:25–16:56).

**What Tan adds:** Tan doesn't make the premium claim. Later in the talk he points to the same mechanism: "this is the kind of like loose network and the spirit of helping each other and this like very long-term outlook has been an awesome thing" (@ 23:35).

**Where this is uncertain:**
- Altman doesn't measure the gap. There are no numbers, and he never says which program is second. The whole reason given is "network effects."
- YC's former president said it at YC's own event, and his "Gary probably can't" admits that conflict of interest.
- The vault's wiki leaf on finding co-founders has this attribution right. It quotes Altman @ 16:56, though it leaves out the "second place" sentence.

**Short answer:** The vault doesn't support that claim, and her recorded view is the opposite. Livingston says early YC deliberately funded *earnest* founders and turned away people it could tell were conceited. She credits that early strictness with shaping YC's culture. No source in the vault has her calling ruthless or aggressive founders the ones who win, so there's no reasoning of hers to explain.

**What she's actually said**
- She judged character while the technical partners judged ideas. What she looked for: "did they seem earnest did they seem determined were they flexible minded and most importantly what was the relationship between the co-founders like" ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s))
- "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" ([@ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s))
- She turned away people she judged conceited: "early on I was pretty rigid about this and I think that's the basis of the culture of our alumni community" ([@ 15:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=927s))
- In 2024 she said the founders she's known are smart, curious, "very determined," and above all independent-minded: "you cannot be conventional minded to start a startup with a brand new idea" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 51:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=3069s))

So the trait she wanted was determination, not ruthlessness. She paired it with earnestness and a working co-founder relationship.

**What she did:** In interviews she usually sat and watched quietly, and afterwards the partners asked her whether to fund the founders. Early on she said no to applicants who seemed conceited. She also admits YC has since funded "some conceited" founders anyway (@ 15:27).

**Short answer:** No. Seibel would tell you to keep the users and the problem, and change the product. Going looking for other people or other problems your MVP could fit is the exact mistake he warns about.

**What Seibel has said** (2019 Startup School talk on planning an MVP, [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM))
- **The rule:** "hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely." ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s))
- **Your situation is the failure mode he names:** "a lot of founders once they've figured out how to build something fall in love with it. And so if it doesn't work for a certain set of users, they start thinking, well, I wonder what other problems this thing can solve." (@ 3:19)
- **His analogy:** "if your screwdriver doesn't help the mechanic solve the problem, keep the mechanic. Keep the problem." (@ 3:53)
- **What to do instead:** "iterate um continue improving on your solution until it actually solves a problem." (@ 3:53)
- **Why you shouldn't be attached to the MVP:** in his Airbnb, Twitch and Stripe examples, "none of the products I showed you before was the initial vision" ([@ 12:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=771s)). An MVP has about the impact of "a paper you wrote in the first grade," so don't fall in love with it.

**What he's done:** Twitch began as Justin.tv, a single-channel reality show. That first product looked nothing like the final one, but they got there by changing the product, not by hunting for a new audience for the original.

**Where this is uncertain**
- **One talk only:** the vault has this view from a single 2019 talk. It has no later Seibel statement updating it, and no rule for when the problem itself turns out not to be real. If your users don't actually care much about the problem, he doesn't cover that case here.
- **One exception, from Paul Graham, not Seibel:** PG (Sept 2026, [essay](https://paulgraham.com/powerful.html)) says that if users are *already* "misusing" your product for something else, "listen for the message they're sending." His example is PayPal. That's different from what you're describing. PG is talking about real users pulling the product toward a need they have. You're describing founders pushing a product out to find a market. If you're actually seeing the first pattern, PG's point applies. If you're just guessing at other markets, Seibel's rule does.

**What to do next, based on the above:** go back to the users you built it for. Find out exactly where the product fails to solve their problem, change it, and put it in front of them again.
